mdxBody:
Asexual reproduction is a straightforward method of creating new plant life. In this process, only one parent plant is involved, and it gives rise to offspring that are essentially clones, sharing the exact genetic makeup of the parent. What makes asexual reproduction distinct is that it doesn't rely on the formation of specialized reproductive cells called gametes or the complex process of meiosis, which shuffles genetic material to produce variation. Instead, asexual reproduction relies on simpler methods, such as cell division or the growth of specialized structures. This simplicity and genetic uniformity make asexual reproduction a reliable and efficient way for some plants to propagate and expand their population. Asexual reproduction includes binary fission, budding, spore formation and vegetative propagation.

## Binary Fission

Binary fission is a simple way of making more of something: it's like splitting something into two equal parts. This method is commonly used for making more of certain tiny living things, like bacteria, some one-celled creatures called protozoa, and some small invertebrates, but no true plant is known to use this process.

In bacteria, first, a copy of their DNA is formed so that there are two identical sets. Then, these sets move to opposite ends of the bacterium. Next, the middle part of the bacterium starts to fold in, dividing the contents into two parts. A new wall forms between these two parts. This whole process ends with two new bacteria, which will keep growing and eventually split into more.

<CaptionedImage src="kg222gk30patgbpmr9hssck6058dqbt6" alt="Diagram showing the steps of binary fission in a bacterium." caption="Fig. 9.1: Binary fission." />
## Budding

In this kind of asexual reproduction, a tiny outgrowth called a bud emerges on the parent's body, like a small bulge. In yeast, a single-celled fungus, this outgrowth forms on one side of the cell. Inside the cell, the nucleus splits into two by mitosis, and one of these new nuclei goes into the outgrowth. Sometimes the parent cell can have more than one outgrowth growing at the same time. Each outgrowth gets bigger and becomes more like the parent. Eventually, the outgrowth can break away from the parent; in other cases, the outgrowths stay attached, leading to groups of individuals living close together, almost like a little community.

<CaptionedImage src="kg21z3m34cw6knzr5zw6vghgtn8dnt01" alt="Diagram of budding in yeast, showing an outgrowth forming on the parent cell." caption="Budding in yeast, a form of asexual reproduction where a new organism develops from an outgrowth or bud due to cell division at one particular site." />

In higher plants, the outgrowths that develop are often of two types: vegetative buds and floral buds. Vegetative buds give rise to new branches and leaves, and floral buds give rise to new flowers.
## Spore Formation

Spores are very small, unicellular, non-motile, thick-walled resistant asexual reproductive bodies. In many fungi, like Rhizopus, when ready to reproduce, body cells create strong, protective sacs called sporangia on the tip of a stalk called a sporangiophore. Inside these sacs, cells divide repeatedly to make many tiny spores. Each spore has a tough shell called a cyst that helps it survive unfavourable conditions. When the sporangia mature, they burst open and release the spores; when conditions become favourable, the spores grow into new Rhizopus.

In unfavourable conditions, some filamentous bacteria, such as actinomycetes, also make spores. These bacterial spores are also thick-walled, and form outside the bacterial cells, so they are called exospores. Upon germination, each spore from a parental filament gives rise to several new bacterial filaments.

It is important to note that the microspores and megaspores of seed-producing plants, and the spores of bryophytes and pteridophytes that give rise to a gametophyte body, are not considered part of asexual reproduction, because meiosis is generally involved in their formation.

<CaptionedImage src="kg21yrqqma722dk8qxtqnzqwjn8dmvn3" alt="Diagram of sporangia forming spores in Rhizopus." caption="Rhizopus (commonly known as black bread mold), depicting its asexual reproductive cycle through spore formation." />

<SideActivity title="Critical Thinking">
Under unfavourable conditions, some species of bacteria reproduce by forming spores, e.g. Clostridium and Bacillus species. These bacterial spores are also thick-walled. They are formed inside bacterial cells, so are called endospores. This way, these bacteria can survive unfavourable periods. When conditions are good, each endospore germinates and resumes normal life. Do you think endospore formation is a reproductive process?
</SideActivity>
## Parthenogenesis

Parthenogenesis is the development of an offspring directly from an unfertilized egg. In flowering plants, it is defined as the asexual formation of a seed from the maternal tissues of the ovule, avoiding the processes of meiosis and fertilization, leading directly to embryo development. This can happen due to various triggers, such as changes in environmental conditions or hormonal signals. Parthenogenesis in plants is also known as apomixis. Since it involves creating offspring without the fusion of genetic material from two parents, it is considered a form of asexual reproduction.

## Vegetative Propagation

Flowering plants generally reproduce sexually by means of their flowers, but some also reproduce without flowers, which we call vegetative propagation. There are two kinds: natural vegetative propagation, which plants do on their own, and artificial vegetative propagation, in which people intervene.

## Natural Vegetative Propagation

Natural vegetative propagation in plants refers to the process by which plants reproduce asexually using their own natural mechanisms, without any human intervention. New plants are generated from various vegetative structures of the parent plant, such as roots, stems, leaves, or specialized structures like runners or bulbs. These structures develop into independent plants, and since they originate from the same parent, they often have identical genetic characteristics.

## Bulbs

Bulbs are compact, thickened, vertically growing, underground stems enveloped by thick, succulent (fleshy) leaves, serving as reservoirs of stored nutrients. Beneath the bulb's base, adventitious roots sprout, while shoots emerge from its upper region. Each shoot can develop into a new plant. Species like tulips, onions, and lilies use bulbs to reproduce.

<CaptionedImage src="kg224p3xb037tgm6rtrtxbrysd8dm8cw" alt="Diagram of a bulb's internal structure." caption="Structural anatomy of an onion bulb." />

The next illustration continues this visual sequence.

<CaptionedImage src="kg2b1cjr9ss6e5b32zjtr4wkah8dnhd6" alt="Diagram of a bulb sprouting a new plant." caption="The structure of a corm, which is an underground modified stem (commonly seen in plants like Colocasia / taro or Gladiolus) adapted for food storage and vegetative propagation." />
## Corms

Corms are compact, thickened, vertically growing underground stems that store food, but are not enveloped by fleshy leaves. Buds at the top of a corm give rise to shoots, which then develop into new plants. Examples of plants that reproduce using corms include dasheen and garlic.

## Rhizomes

Rhizomes are flat, horizontal underground stems that have small scale-like leaves. Along the rhizome are distinct nodes and internodes; buds form at these nodes. Buds on the upper side of the rhizome grow into shoots, while the lower side produces adventitious roots. These shoots can develop into new plants. Plants like ginger, ferns, and water lilies use rhizomes to reproduce.

<CaptionedImage src="kg28hetsvngqaatg5frmh70pqx8dmtck" alt="Diagram of a rhizome showing nodes with shoots and roots." caption="Rhizome, which is a horizontal underground modified stem (such as in ginger or turmeric)" />
## Stem Tubers

Stem tubers are swollen tips of underground stems that primarily serve as storage structures in certain plants. Stem tubers often have "eyes" or bud clusters on their surface, from which new shoots can grow when conditions are suitable. Examples include potatoes and yams; these structures serve both as a food source and a means of propagation.

<CaptionedImage src="kg2cjrsx21bzx86k0w49v72ay18dn384" alt="Diagram of a potato stem tuber showing eyes/buds." caption="vegetative propagation in a potato plant using underground stem tubers." />
## Stolons or Runners

The above-ground parts of plants like strawberries and creeping buttercups are typically very short, with most of their structure below ground; these short stems are called rootstocks, and carry leaves and flowers. After the main shoot has bloomed, side buds create long shoots that grow horizontally along the ground, called stolons or runners. These runners have small scale-like leaves at specific points (nodes), with long internodes between them. At each node there is a bud that can grow into both a shoot and roots, so a whole new plant can develop there, getting nourishment from the parent plant through the runner for a while. Eventually the runner dries up and withers away, leaving a new independent plant growing a short distance from the parent. This is how a strawberry plant, for example, can make many new plants without using seeds.

<CaptionedImage src="kg2dhspgpvv4k70g5jw5acqn998dn8xk" alt="Diagram of a strawberry plant producing runners." caption="Asexual reproduction in a strawberry plant using horizontal stems called runners (or stolons)." />

The next illustration continues this visual sequence.

<CaptionedImage src="kg273bx2wp560fdq42vhah921s8dnc3q" alt="Diagram of a new plantlet forming at a runner's node." caption="Vegetative propagation by suckers (or root shoots) in a blackberry plant." />
## Suckers

Suckers typically emerge as small shoots from the underground parts of a plant, such as the root system or near the base of the main stem. These shoots can develop into new plants; as suckers grow, they form their own stems, leaves, and roots, essentially becoming self-sustaining plants while remaining connected to the parent plant for a period. Suckers may receive nutrients and water from the parent plant, helping them establish themselves, which is especially beneficial in adverse conditions. Over time, suckers develop their own root system and become less dependent on the parent plant, eventually thriving independently. Suckers are a common method of natural vegetative propagation in various ground cover plants such as lawn grass.

## Vegetative Propagation by Leaves

In Bryophyllum, new plantlets are created along the edges of its leaves. These plantlets are like tiny versions of the parent plant. When they detach from the parent plant and fall onto the soil below, they can grow and develop into separate, self-sustaining plants.

## Methods of Artificial Vegetative Propagation

Artificial vegetative propagation is adapted when people purposely grow plants to meet specific needs. The part of the plant used for this is called a "vegetative propagule." These methods help preserve the good qualities of plants, like taste, colour, and disease resistance. Two common methods of artificial vegetative propagation are stem cuttings and grafting.

## Stem Cuttings

Stem cuttings are small segments or cut pieces of stem having at least one node. New plants can be grown from some plants by placing a cut piece of stem in water or damp soil: roots start growing from the bottom of the stem into the soil, while the top part keeps growing and making leaves. If a cutting does not start growth, the cut ends can be treated with a plant hormone called auxin to stimulate growth. Sometimes the top part of the cutting is covered with plastic or a glass jar to reduce water loss. This method is often used to propagate roses, ivy, grapevines, and chrysanthemums.

<CaptionedImage src="kg2b6h58pd3b3g573nr15akr698dmvcq" alt="Diagram of a stem cutting rooting in soil." caption="vegetative propagation using stem cuttings" />
## Grafting

This method involves joining two plant parts together to create a single, new plant. It is commonly used to reproduce desirable plant varieties, like fruit trees or ornamental plants, and it's a skilled practice often performed by gardeners and farmers.

Two plant parts are involved in grafting: the scion and the rootstock. The scion is the upper part of the plant, carrying the desired characteristics, such as specific fruit or flower traits. The rootstock is the lower part, which provides the root system and stem support. A skilled gardener makes precise cuts on both the scion and rootstock, usually at specific angles to maximize contact between the two parts. The scion is carefully attached to the rootstock; this connection is crucial for the transport of water, nutrients, and other substances between the two parts. To ensure a secure connection, the graft is typically bound with grafting tape, rubber bands, or other materials, which helps hold the scion in place until the graft heals. Once the graft has healed, the plant begins to grow, producing leaves, flowers, and fruit based on the characteristics of the scion.

<CaptionedImage src="kg2450hb7wn6sw6pq5q7dvq7ah8dm6jf" alt="Diagram showing the scion and rootstock being joined in grafting." caption="Selected image illustrates grafting, an artificial method of vegetative (asexual) plant propagation." />

The next illustration continues this visual sequence.

<CaptionedImage src="kg25pxzs1kjhpc7b41p5v1344s8dncts" alt="Diagram of a healed graft union." caption="Plant tissue culture (micropropagation) using a carrot to grow new plants from a small tissue sample." />
## Cloning (Tissue Culturing)

Cloning is a method of producing genetically identical individuals from a single parental cell. In plants, the term "cloning" refers to tissue culturing, in which a single plant cell or piece of tissue is grown on artificial nutrient medium under aseptic (microbe-free) conditions to develop a genetically identical copy (clone) of the parent plant. This method of artificial vegetative propagation is also called micropropagation. The first cell or tiny piece of the parent plant used in tissue culture is called an "explant." This explant is placed on a special nutrient medium to grow into an undifferentiated mass of cells known as "callus." The callus is then treated with different substances to make it produce shoots and later roots, resulting in a young plant called a "plantlet." These plantlets are carefully moved into soil in their natural surroundings to continue growing.

<SideActivity title="Critical Thinking">
Sweet potato is an enlarged root. Farmers place it in moist sand or soil until it produces several plantlets. Then the plantlets are removed and planted. This process is used to produce many plants from a single plant. Is it artificial or natural vegetative propagation, and which type does it belong to?
</SideActivity>

title: 9.1 Asexual Reproduction

mdxBody:
## Sexual Reproduction Across Plant Groups

Sexual reproduction in plants, like in animals, involves the fertilization of gametes (egg and sperm) and formation of a zygote and embryo. Different groups of plants, like bryophytes, pteridophytes, and seed plants (spermatophytes), have different mechanisms of gamete formation and fertilization. In bryophytes and pteridophytes, the sperms are like little swimmers: they can move around and find the egg cells, so they need water to do this (it could be dew or rain). Seed-producing plants (gymnosperms and angiosperms), on the other hand, don't rely on water to get their sperm to the egg cells; they have their own special techniques, covered further in this chapter.

One of the prominent features of plants is the haplo-diplontic lifecycle, i.e. a haploid gametophyte (gamete-producing plant body) generation and a diploid sporophyte (spore-producing plant body) generation that regularly alternate with each other during the lifecycle. In some plants like bryophytes, the gametophyte generation is more prominent (dominant) while the sporophyte is much reduced. In the rest of the plant kingdom, the sporophyte is the dominant generation, while the gametophyte is a very small structure.

## Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants (Angiosperms)

In flowering plants (angiosperms), the major plant body is the sporophyte, which may be a herb, shrub, or tree. Flowers are the reproductive parts of these plants.

## Structure of a Flower

A flower is like a plant's special tool for making new plants: a part of the plant changed and adapted for reproduction. A flower generally consists of a stalk called the pedicel, like the flower's stem, holding it up. At the top of the pedicel is a swollen part called the thalamus, like the flower's platform. The thalamus generally bears four kinds of parts called floral leaves, arranged in whorls (circles) on its upper surface.

The outermost circle is the calyx, made up of green leaves called sepals, a protective cover for the inside parts of the flower. Just inside the calyx is another circle, the corolla, consisting of variously coloured floral leaves called petals. Deeper inside is the androecium, the male parts of the flower, called stamens, important for making pollen. Right in the centre is the gynoecium, where the female parts are, in something called the carpel or pistil, where new seeds start to form.

<CaptionedImage src="kg23y4yqrfkqs5s3dn5yth8e518dnwy1" alt="Diagram of a flower's structure showing calyx, corolla, androecium, and gynoecium." caption="anatomy of a typical bisexual flower" />

The calyx and corolla, the outer two circles, are like the flower's protectors: they keep everything safe inside but do not take part in reproduction directly, so they are called accessory whorls. The androecium and gynoecium, the inner two circles, are the ones that actually make the flower's reproduction happen, so they are called necessary whorls.
## Formation of Microspores and Megaspores

Each stamen consists of a long stalk, the filament, and a bilobed swollen tip called the anther. In the anther lobes, four pollen sacs (microsporangia) are present, which produce haploid pollen grains (microspores) by meiosis.

Each carpel or pistil consists of a sac-like structure at the bottom called the ovary, a long tubular structure above the ovary called the style, and a swollen tip on the style called the stigma. The ovary contains one to numerous ovules (megasporangia). Each ovule possesses one spore mother cell that undergoes meiosis to produce four megaspores; of these four, only one is capable of surviving further and becomes the functional megaspore.

## Pollination

When microspores are formed, the wall of the pollen sacs bursts and the microspores are liberated. The microspores are transferred from the anther of the stamen to the stigma of the carpel by wind, insects, or other animals; this event is called pollination, and the microspores during pollination are called pollen grains. If pollination occurs within the same flower or between two flowers of the same plant, it is called self-pollination; if it occurs between two flowers of separate plants, it is called cross pollination, which ensures more genetic variability in coming generations.

| Table 9.1: Adaptations in insect-pollinated and wind-pollinated flowers |  |  |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Feature | Insect Pollinated Flowers | Wind Pollinated Flowers |
| Size | Generally large | Generally small |
| Colour | Petals brightly coloured | Petals green or dull in colour |
| Nectar | Produce nectar | Do not produce nectar |
| Floral arrangement | Flowers face upwards | Flowers hang down for easy shaking |
| Stamens and stigmas | Enclosed inside ring of petals | Hang out of ring of petals |
| Pollen grains | Small number produced, heavy and sticky | Large number produced, light with smooth surface |
| Stigma | Pinhead shaped with no branches | Feathery branches for catching pollen |

<SideActivity title="Critical Thinking">
Sometimes pesticides are used to control the attack of insect pests on crops. Although pesticides are quite effective at preventing loss from insect pests, farmers sometimes still get a lower yield than normal. Why is this so?
</SideActivity>

## Development of Male Gametophyte

After pollination, the microspores (pollen grains) germinate on the surface of the stigma to produce a male gametophyte. In this process, the microspore nucleus first divides by mitosis to form two nuclei, the tube nucleus and the generative nucleus, which divides further to form two sperm nuclei. The tube nucleus controls the formation of the pollen tube, which passes down through the style and ultimately penetrates the ovule. This whole structure, comprising the microspore body, pollen tube, tube nucleus, and the two sperm nuclei, is referred to as the male gametophyte.

## Development of Female Gametophyte

Meanwhile, the nucleus of the functional megaspore at the centre of the ovule divides three times by mitosis to make 8 nuclei. Three of these eight nuclei migrate to one end of the ovule; the central one becomes the egg, and the two flanking it are called synergids. Three other nuclei migrate to the other end of the ovule, and act as antipodals. The remaining two daughter nuclei rest at the centre of the ovule and are called polar nuclei, which in some cases fuse together to become a diploid secondary nucleus before the sperm enters. This whole structure, comprising the body of the megaspore, three antipodals, two synergids, two polar nuclei (or the secondary nucleus), and an egg, is referred to as the female gametophyte, or embryo sac.

## Fertilization and the Formation of Zygote and Endosperm Nucleus

When the pollen tube penetrates the ovule, one sperm nucleus fuses with the egg to form a diploid zygote, and the other sperm nucleus fuses with the polar nuclei (or secondary nucleus) to make a triploid endosperm nucleus. Since one male gametophyte contributes two sperm nuclei for fertilization, this event is called double fertilization. It is assumed that the rest of the nuclei in the embryo sac, such as the synergids and antipodals, control the process of fertilization.

<SideActivity title="Critical Thinking">
Why is fertilization in angiosperms called double fertilization?
</SideActivity>

## Seed and Fruit Formation

After fertilization, the ovule is transformed into a seed, so it is defined as a "ripened ovule", while the surrounding wall of the ovary is transformed into fruit, so it is defined as a "ripened ovary".

<CaptionedImage src="kg28dw8vvmpyrc91n98fzwbeys88x9nr" alt="Diagram showing an ovule ripening into a seed and the ovary wall ripening into fruit." caption="Fig. 9.15: Seed and fruit formation." />

## Structure of Seed

Angiosperm seeds are made up of three important parts:

1. **Embryo**: This part comes from the union of male and female cells (zygote): a baby plant that's not yet fully grown.
2. **Endosperm**: A storage space for food, formed from a special cell inside the seed.
3. **Seed Coat**: The seed's protective jacket, developing from the outer layer that used to wrap around the seed when it was part of the plant.

The seed coat can be thin like paper (as in peanuts) or thick and tough (as in coconuts). It keeps the baby plant safe from harm and stops it from drying out. There's a mark on the seed coat called the hilum, where the seed used to be connected to the plant. Nearby is the micropyle, a small opening the seed uses to take in water.

Inside the seed, the embryo is an immature plant, consisting of a radicle, a plumule, and one or two cotyledons (seed leaves). The radicle of the embryo grows into the new root, while the plumule grows into the new shoot upon germination; radicle and plumule are therefore called the embryonic root and embryonic stem respectively. The embryonic stem above the point of attachment of the cotyledon(s) is called the epicotyl; the embryonic stem below that point is the hypocotyl. Within the seed there is a store of nutrients for the growing seedling; in angiosperms, this stored food is derived from the endosperm tissue, rich in oil or starch and protein. In many seeds, the food of the endosperm is absorbed and stored by the cotyledons.

<CaptionedImage src="kg2cktfw0mfht752t32vb3ebb188w99x" alt="Diagram of seed structure showing embryo, endosperm, and seed coat." caption="Fig. 9.16: Structure of a seed." />

<SideActivity title="Critical Thinking">
Why are angiosperms called closed-seeded plants?
</SideActivity>

<SideActivity title="Science Tidbit">
Based on the number of cotyledons and some other features, angiosperms are classified into two classes: monocots and dicots.
</SideActivity>

## Seed Germination

For seeds to start growing, they need to be in the right place at the right time; this process is called seed germination, the start of a plant's life. The seed absorbs water, which makes it swell and breaks open the seed coat. First, a root pops out from the radicle; this root grows quickly and starts taking in water and nutrients from the soil. Then a tiny shoot called the plumule begins to grow, stretching up and out of the soil. There are two main ways seeds can start growing:

<SideActivity title="STEAM Activity 9.1">
Take a few seeds of commonly growing plants in your vicinity, plant them together in a pot, and observe the germination process day by day, picking one germinating seed to examine every day.
</SideActivity>

## Epigeal Germination

In this type, the hypocotyl stretches out and forms a hook, pulling the seed leaves (cotyledons) above the ground. Beans, cotton, and papaya are examples of seeds that germinate this way.

## Hypogeal Germination

Here, it's the epicotyl that stretches and forms a hook, but the seed leaves (cotyledons) stay underground. Peas, maize, and coconuts are examples of seeds that germinate this way.

## Conditions for Seed Germination

For seeds to start growing, they need the right conditions, both inside and outside. Inside, the seed must have a living baby plant (embryo) and enough stored food.

Outside, there are three key conditions:

1. **Water (Moisture)**: Most seeds have very little water inside them; they can't start growing until they soak up water from the environment, which is used to break down stored food and help the baby plant's parts grow.
2. **Oxygen**: Just as we need oxygen to breathe, the cells in the baby plant need it too, to carry out their functions.
3. **Temperature**: Different seeds prefer different temperatures to start growing; for most plants, the best temperature is between 25-30°C.

<CaptionedImage src="kg21dh8v94jjbt3mdw5fr6j4r98dmh65" alt="Diagram of conditions needed for seed germination: water, oxygen, and temperature." caption="the two main types of seed germination: Epigeal and Hypogeal." />

When a seed gets these conditions right, it's like a green light for the baby plant to begin its journey.

<SideActivity title="Lab Activity: Flower Encounters - Secrets of Plant Reproduction">
Investigate the structure of flowers and gain insights into the reproductive mechanisms of plants.

**Materials:** Assorted flowers (various species), scalpels or small knives, disposable gloves, magnifying glasses, petri dishes or small trays, notebooks and pens, camera or smartphones for documentation.

**Procedure:**

1. Begin by discussing the significance of flowers in plant reproduction and the different parts of a typical flower (petals, sepals, stamens, pistil).
2. Distribute various types of flowers to students, ensuring a diverse selection.
3. Provide disposable gloves and scalpels or small knives for flower dissection, emphasizing safety precautions during handling of cutting tools.
4. Instruct students to carefully dissect the flowers, identifying and observing each part, focusing on the arrangement of reproductive structures within the pistil and stamens.
5. Encourage students to use magnifying glasses or take photos for closer examination, sketch the dissected flowers in their notebooks, and paste the floral parts on a hard chart to make herbarium sheets.

Ask students to identify specific adaptations related to attracting pollinators and achieving successful fertilization, compare their findings, and discuss similarities and differences in flower anatomy. Discuss observed variations in flower structure among different species and how these variations contribute to successful pollination, linking observed structures to the process of seed and fruit formation. Discuss the relation between overuse of insecticide by farmers and insect pollinators in plant reproduction. Conclude by reinforcing the role of flowers as essential components of the plant life cycle.
</SideActivity>
